title: Actually, maybe: How German Angst could become Europe’s nightmare - European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Germany is losing 15,000 industrial jobs a month under a paralyzed Merz government, and imminent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt could hand the far-right AfD its first outright governing majority in a German state - a domestic crisis the authors argue would directly threaten the EU's budget, industrial policy, rearmament and Ukraine support given Germany's central economic and political weight.

insights.claim: Polling suggests the far-right AfD could win an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt's September 6, 2026 state election, with the AfD, CDU and Left potentially the only parties to clear the 5% parliamentary threshold - which would give the AfD control of a German state government for the first time.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel, Jana Puglierin
insights.so_what: A first-ever AfD state government would be a watershed test of Germany's political 'firewall' and a leading indicator of far-right momentum ahead of subsequent Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern elections.
insights.locator: Why the Angst is now real

insights.claim: The CDU's collapsing preferred coalition partner, the Free Democrats (now polling below 5% almost everywhere), combined with the CDU's refusal to cooperate with the AfD, is increasingly locking the CDU into dependency on centre-left coalitions - a dynamic that is fueling internal CDU pressure to question the anti-AfD 'firewall.'
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel, Jana Puglierin
insights.so_what: Structural coalition-math pressure, not just ideology, is eroding the CDU's willingness to maintain its cordon sanitaire against the AfD.
insights.locator: Many in the CDU are frustrated

insights.claim: The AfD's platform includes drastically curbing immigration and asylum, reversing key elements of the energy transition, challenging European integration, ending the euro, and pursuing a nationalist foreign policy - and the party is described as a symptom of establishment failure rather than its cause, having built support over more than a decade before now nearing actual power.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel, Jana Puglierin
insights.so_what: An AfD with real governing power would directly threaten German participation in the euro and EU integration commitments, a tail risk for eurozone stability.
insights.quote: The strength of the AfD is a symptom, not a cause.

insights.claim: Germany is losing approximately 15,000 industrial jobs per month amid six years of weak growth, rising Chinese competition, US tariffs and energy price shocks, and the authors describe this as the material basis for the AfD's rise rather than mere political dissatisfaction.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel, Jana Puglierin
insights.so_what: A concrete, trackable monthly industrial-job-loss figure that functions as a leading indicator for both German political risk and further deindustrialization pressure on German manufacturers and suppliers.
insights.quote: A Germany that is oozing 15,000 industrial jobs each month

insights.claim: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government has made more reform announcements than actual reforms, continuing a pattern from the prior government's failed attempt to adapt to the 'Zeitenwende' without imposing hardship on Germans, and the authors argue the government is now equally unable to muster the political strength for major reform.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel, Jana Puglierin
insights.so_what: Suggests investors should discount German reform announcements as a policy catalyst until actual legislative delivery is confirmed.
insights.locator: In recent years, German leaders have made more reform announcements

insights.claim: The one policy area where Merz's government is shifting toward a tougher stance is China, pushing a more active European position on protecting markets from Chinese 'predatory' economic behavior - and Merz himself credited this shift not to his own political leadership but to a changed posture within the German auto industry.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel, Jana Puglierin
insights.so_what: Signals that German China policy is being driven by industry lobbying rather than top-down government strategy, useful for anticipating the direction and durability of EU-China trade measures.

themes.theme: Why a German crisis is a European crisis

insights.claim: The authors' central thesis is that Germany's economic and political weight, its role at the heart of the EU, and its status as the bloc's most populous member state mean a German political crisis would drag Europe toward fragmentation, threatening the EU's next Multiannual Financial Framework, industrial policy, rearmament and resilience efforts, autonomous-technology capacity, global trade leverage, and continued support for Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel, Jana Puglierin
insights.so_what: Frames German domestic political risk as a direct, near-term threat to EU-level budget, rearmament and Ukraine-support timelines - a macro-relevant transmission channel for investors tracking European policy risk.
insights.quote: Unless political leaders come up with something new, a German pall will blot all major items on the EU's agenda

insights.claim: A Swedish official is quoted saying 'German leadership is not optional,' while German political elites appear to disagree - despite Germany being the world's third-largest economy at the core of the world's largest single market, with leading global companies and one of the largest defense budgets anywhere.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel, Jana Puglierin
insights.so_what: Highlights a leadership-vacuum gap between Germany's objective economic/military capacity and its actual willingness to exercise agency - a key variable for whether the EU can respond decisively to simultaneous crises.

insights.claim: Germany was previously labeled 'the sick man of Europe' in 1999 before recovering to become the continent's exporting powerhouse, but the authors argue this time may be different because the AfD is now within striking distance of actual governing power rather than remaining in opposition.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel, Jana Puglierin
insights.so_what: Cautions against assuming Germany will simply repeat its post-1999 recovery pattern, given the qualitatively different political risk of far-right governing power this cycle.
insights.locator: Germany is hardly the first European country
